summary: After a mutating request returns 2xx, compare the response object against the fields that were sent. When nothing sent comes back, the write did not apply -- fail the command (flat --stdin bodies) or warn (everything else). Adds the --verify-writes global flag.
reason:
form-encode-rails-bracket-params fixed the flag path, where the generated tree builds Rails bracket names. It deliberately left --stdin on the JSON path, because a genuine nested JSON document is the one body shape Canvas accepts as JSON and it was the only way to write through this CLI before that patch.

That leaves --stdin unguarded. It unmarshals whatever JSON it is handed and ships it verbatim, with no knowledge of what the endpoint expects. Rails builds params from the names it recognizes and silently drops the rest, so a body like {"wiki_page_body": "..."} -- a plausible-looking flattening of wiki_page[body] -- is accepted with HTTP 200 and the unmodified page. The CLI printed a success envelope containing a page object, and the caller reasonably read that as proof.

This was observed in the field: an agent asked to darken low-contrast text on a course front page sent exactly that body, got 200, reported the change as done, and the page was untouched. It only recovered because it re-fetched and compared byte counts by hand. An agent that trusted the exit code would have reported a fix that never happened.

Predicting the accepted parameter names per endpoint is not available at the client -- the bracket names live in the 1,180 generated command files and --stdin bypasses them entirely. So the check runs from the other direction: reduce the request body to the leaf field names a resource would carry (wiki_page[body] and {"wiki_page":{"body":..}} both reduce to "body"), then look for any of them as keys on the returned object. One hit is enough to conclude the controller understood the request. Zero hits means the parameters were dropped.

Severity is keyed to body shape, which is what makes the check safe to fail on. A flat map with no bracket key and no nested value is the shape --stdin produces when the caller guessed at names, and no Canvas write endpoint takes its parameters that way; that is a hard finding and exits non-zero. Bracketed bodies (built from flags) and nested bodies (correct --stdin) only ever warn, because real endpoints legitimately accept parameters they do not echo -- course[event], wiki_page[notify_of_update] -- and a false failure on those would be worse than a missed no-op.

When a flat key splits into a prefix and a suffix that is a real field on the returned resource, the message names the bracket parameter it was probably meant to be and both ways to send it. wiki_page_body against a page response yields wiki_page[body], the --stdin nesting, and --wiki-page-body.

Upstream: the generator knows each endpoint's parameter names at print time and should validate a --stdin body against them before sending, which would catch this at the call site with a better message than a response-shape heuristic can give. This patch is the client-side floor that holds regardless.
known_limitations:
The check proves the controller parsed the parameters, not that the resource changed. A write whose field names are echoed but whose values the server rejected, normalized, or clamped still reads as applied. Value comparison was tried and dropped: Canvas sanitizes HTML on save, so a wiki_page[body] round-trip legitimately differs from what was sent, and comparing values produced false failures on correct writes. Confirming a value landed still requires a re-read, which is why the skill instructs agents to do that.

Severity is inferred from body shape, so a bracketed or nested body that Canvas ignored only warns. That is deliberate -- see the reason field -- but it means the hard failure covers exactly the --stdin misuse case and nothing else.

Responses that are not a JSON object are skipped entirely: bulk endpoints returning an array, 204s with an empty body, and binary responses carry no resource to compare against. Deletes usually fall in this group.

The flattened-bracket suggestion reads the response for its field list, so it only appears when the endpoint returns the resource. It prefers the longest prefix (wiki_page[body] over wiki[page_body]), which is right for Canvas's naming but is a heuristic, not a lookup.

--verify-writes=off restores the previous behavior verbatim if any of this proves wrong in the field.
validated_outcome:
Verified against the live Canvas instance that produced the original report (course 88, page aiinfra-101-development-environments-and-tools).

Before: `pages update --stdin` with {"wiki_page_body": ...} exited 0 and printed a page object; the page was unchanged.

After: the same invocation exits 5 with 'returned success but the write did not apply', names both sent keys, identifies wiki_page[body] as the intended parameter, and prints the --stdin nesting and the --wiki-page-body flag. Controls confirm no regression: the same page written through --wiki-page-body exits 0 silently, and through correctly nested --stdin ({"wiki_page":{"body":...}}) exits 0 silently.

Unit tests cover applied writes (bracket, nested, multi-field, partially-echoed), the flattened-key finding and its message, the soft finding for an unechoed bracket parameter, every not-enough-information case (nil/empty/non-map body, array/empty/non-JSON/scalar response), leaf-name reduction across bracket shapes, longest-prefix suggestion, body-shape classification, and flag parsing. Full Go suite passes (7 packages). golangci-lint introduces no new findings against the pre-change baseline and clears one pre-existing gofmt issue.
